title: Individuals versus group names in rock-era marketing
summary: Ridley asks, with George Russell's view, whether group emphasis replaced individuality.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: So do you--I'm not trying to lead you but I'm just trying to sort of put it into uh, a certain kind of thing of what I think I hear you say in terms of--you know, and it's still trying to tie it back to the whole thing of defining what is jazz. One of the things that you said, you mentioned about repetition and how they don't seem to have no imagination, you just keep repeating the same thing over and over again and how it doesn't seem to have any imagination--and you say why can't you come up with something else, like you say a channel might be put in with some--different might happen--show some imagination. Would you say that the concept of individuality, I mean, people trying to be individuals was more of a kind of focus that was happening say up until say about the Forties and Fifties and even

a part of the early Sixties and then things started turning around to a more of a group kind of thing where it's, like you say, more a mass appeal kind of sound and concept? You know, like, OK, I'll tell you where I'm coming from. George Russell, who we both know very well, you know, as done a lot as far as trying to come up with like a lot of theoretical concepts about getting jazz musicians to become more sophisticated, harmony with "Cubano Bee, Cubano Bop" with Dizzy.... and stuff like that./..George Russell seems to think that at one point there was a thing like you come-- like you say, yourself, you Sam Jones coming from Tampa Florida, Charlie Parker coming from Kansas City, Miles Davis coming from Alton, Illinois, so forth and so on, coming to New York to make your mark as an individualist. Whereas he seems to think, when the rock groups started being pushed commercially then suddenly he was more about a group emphasis. Instead of hearing about individuals, you started hearing about groups, suddenly there was the Nuggets and the Eggheads and the, all this and other. It wasn't so much a, an emphasis on looking at the individuals in the group but it was a group kind of thing. Just like if we say now, Weather Report , when most people say the weather report, they don't think so much of Joe Zawinul, or Wayne Shorter, ah, the little boy that plays the bass guitar, Jaco, they think of the weather report, you know. It seems like the emphasis is--do you agree with that? I mean, do you think that has had any in-

fluence cause trying to figure out what has caused these different intracies. It seems like there is a lot of confusion going on with a lot of people. Like you said, the program directors, the people up there who are programming what they say is jazz and they don't, in your estimation and in mine also, they ain't playing no jazz. But do you think this is possibly some of it; have an influence, this idea of group orientation as opposed to individuals.
